source_text: Quod cum ingratis, concesseris, sequitur tot rerum bonarum, corporum, sexuum, coniunctionum, malos fructus esse non posse Qui autem corpora fecerat, divisit et sexum: divisit in specie, quod in operatione coniungeret; fecitque causam coniunctionum dissimilitudo membrorum Deus bonus, per quem facta sunt omnia, ipse corporis nostri membra formavit
pass_a_gloss: That/which when/with ingratis, concesseris, sequitur so-many rerum bonarum, of-bodies, of-the-sexes, coniunctionum, evil fruit to-be not to-be-able who however bodies fecerat, divisit and six: divisit in specie, that/which in operatione coniungeret; made-and case coniunctionum dissimilitudo of-members God good, through whom made are all-things, himself of-the-body nostri members formavit.
pass_b_english: The good God, through whom everything was made, himself formed the parts of our body.
He who made bodies also distinguished the sexes. He made them different in form in order to join them in action; the difference between their organs supplied the reason for their union.
Therefore the union of bodies comes from the same source as bodies themselves.
Once you have conceded this, however unwillingly, it follows that so many good things—bodies, sexes, unions—cannot have evil fruits.

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Contra Iulianum / Against Julian), including authorities Julian quoted; Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
